clue.text: Bobby the editor? That's uninspired

parts.note: a bobby is a British policeman, in old slang a flatfoot
ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: Someone sneers that the newspaper editor is a dull, plodding sort.
explanation.walkthrough: A bobby is the British nickname for a police officer; FLATFOOT is older American slang for the same beat cop.
explanation.definitionFit: Being caught flat-footed means being unready and pedestrian, so the word describes something dull and lacking imagination.

clue.text: Pretence is far from bold

explanation.surface: A claim of strength is in fact timid.
explanation.definitionFit: A feint is a deceptive move, and feint lines on paper are faint and light, the opposite of heavy type.

clue.text: Monkey about to hang — on silver tail?

indicators.note: about means going around, so the ape wraps the other pieces

parts.note: an ape is a monkey in loose usage
pend means to hang, as in pendant and pending
AG is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A primate is about to dangle from a silver tail.
explanation.definitionFit: An appendage is something attached to the end of a body, as a tail is.

clue.text: Getting personal impressions of a typist's job

explanation.surface: A clerk earns a living taking personal impressions.
explanation.definitionFit: Police take ink marks of a suspect's fingers for identity, and a typist literally prints with fingers.

clue.text: No sense can be got from this agreement

indicators.note: can be got from says the letters of no sense can be rearranged to give something new

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone claims sense cannot be extracted from this accord.
explanation.definitionFit: Oneness is unity, being of one mind, which is harmony between people.

clue.text: Author of revelations, a retired artist's model?

parts.note: ex means former, retired from a role
a poser is someone who poses, as a model does for a painter

explanation.surface: A former life model writes a revealing memoir.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who exposes secrets is a revealer of hidden truths.

clue.text: A Dean's work among the rich

indicators.note: among says the letters sit inside the run of words the rich

explanation.surface: A churchman's writings circulate among wealthy people.
explanation.walkthrough: Dean Farrar, a Victorian clergyman, wrote the moral school story titled with this boy's name, subtitled Little by Little.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian Dean Frederic Farrar wrote a famous school novel bearing this title.

clue.text: "… that spare Cassius. He — much" (J. Caesar).

definitions.text: "… that spare Cassius. He — much" (J. Caesar).

parts.words: "… that spare Cassius. He — much" (J. Caesar).
parts.note: a fill in the blank from Shakespeare, where Caesar distrusts lean Cassius, saying he studies books a great deal

explanation.surface: A quotation from Julius Caesar with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Caesar says of Cassius that he has a lean and hungry look and spends much time with books; supply the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar's line is that Cassius pores over books much, so the missing verb means studies books.

clue.text: Took counsel for granted

explanation.surface: Advice was sought and then taken as given.
explanation.definitionFit: To confer is to consult together, and also to bestow an honour.

clue.text: Not much in the end for the plank-walker

definitions.text: in the end for the plank-walker

explanation.surface: The pirate's victim ends up in a small way at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny amount is a negligible portion, and a pirate's victim forced off the plank falls into the sea.

clue.text: One member elected, say, is back to make impact

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
MP is a Member of Parliament
in means elected, as a party gets in

indicators.note: is back tells us the abbreviation for say is written backwards

parts.note: say means for example, abbreviated EG

explanation.surface: A newly elected MP returns to Westminster determined to make an impression.
explanation.definitionFit: To impinge is to strike or have an effect upon something.

clue.text: To "belong", a French marshal entertains a king

indicators.note: entertains means holding a guest within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Philippe Petain was a Marshal of France
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A French military commander hosts royalty to show they are welcome.
explanation.definitionFit: To pertain to something is to be connected with it or to be part of it.

clue.text: They offer to supply harbour vessels without hesitation

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside means the vessels wrap round the hesitation

parts.note: tenders are small boats serving ships in harbour
er is the sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: Small boats in the port are kept supplied promptly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking, so the hesitation sits within the boats.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who submit tenders are bidders offering to provide goods or services.

clue.text: The Head, holding pole, or stick

indicators.note: holding means the head word contains the pole letter

parts.note: pate is an old word for the head
S is the south pole

explanation.surface: A headteacher grips a pole or a cane.
explanation.definitionFit: Paste is glue, and to paste is to make things adhere.

clue.text: A pile of potatoes — or merely a , brace?

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a heap of spuds is merely a support.
explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper text has a stray comma before 'brace'. In Britain a clamp is a heap of root crops stored under straw and earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A clamp is a covered mound for storing root vegetables, and also a gripping device that holds things together.

clue.text: Josh, getting short measure with a bird

parts.note: to josh is to tease, which is to chaff
an inch is a short unit of length

explanation.surface: Someone named Josh is shortchanged when buying a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The chaffinch is a common European finch.

clue.text: Singer on a romantically unusual errand, see!

indicators.note: an unusual arrangement, romantically, says the letters of the next words are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A vocalist sets out on a strange, romantic mission, behold!
explanation.definitionFit: A serenader sings love songs, traditionally beneath a window at night.

clue.text: Once the penny is dropped, it's out

parts.note: D was the symbol for the old British penny before decimalisation
missed means dropped, as with a catch

explanation.surface: When the coin falls the light dawns, but it has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: D stood for the pre-1971 British penny. 'The penny dropped' looks like an idiom for understanding.
explanation.definitionFit: A batter who is out in cricket has been sent back to the pavilion.

clue.text: Parties — if possible, with drinks

indicators.note: possible suggests one possible arrangement of the letters of the words before it

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Gatherings, if you can manage it, should come with something to drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Aperitifs are alcoholic drinks taken before a meal to stimulate appetite.

clue.text: Lehar — in trouble with his nose?

indicators.note: trouble suggests disorder, so the composer's name and in are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The composer of The Merry Widow suffers some nasal complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: Franz Lehar was an operetta composer; the clue imagines him with a blocked nose needing a device.
explanation.definitionFit: An inhaler is a device for breathing medicine in, used for a stuffy nose.

clue.text: Thus fortifies with comforts

parts.note: so means thus
to lace a drink is to fortify it with spirits

explanation.surface: Someone strengthens their resolve with creature comforts.
explanation.definitionFit: Solaces are consolations, sources of relief in distress.

clue.text: Watered the garden wearing stockings

explanation.surface: Someone did the watering in their tights.
explanation.definitionFit: Hosed means sprayed with a garden hose, and also clad in hose, an old word for stockings.

clue.text: Type set in spring

explanation.surface: A printing font is fixed in the season of spring.
explanation.walkthrough: Fount is the British spelling of font, a set of type in one style and size.
explanation.definitionFit: A fount is a complete set of printing type of one face, and also a poetic word for a fountain or source.

clue.text: Discourage a gangster by cutting off his head

indicators.note: cutting off his head removes the first letter of the gangster word

parts.note: a gunman is an armed gangster

explanation.surface: A mobster is deterred by decapitation.
explanation.definitionFit: To unman someone is to sap their courage, to dishearten them.

clue.text: Albert's place due for sanctification

parts.note: the Royal Albert Hall is the famous London concert hall
owing means due to be paid

explanation.surface: A concert venue named after Albert is earmarked for a blessing ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Albert Hall is a large concert venue in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Hallowing means making holy or consecrating, which is what sanctification is.

clue.text: Frivolous — my kind of aunt

explanation.surface: Someone describes their aunt as silly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My giddy aunt!' is a dated British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Giddy means flighty and light-hearted, and 'my giddy aunt' is an old exclamation.

clue.text: Man tangling with lion for so low a fee?

indicators.note: tangling with suggests a mixing up of the letters of man and lion together

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks who would wrestle a lion for such small payment.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition works through the phrase 'a nominal fee', one so small it is a token.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominal charge is a token amount, far below the real value.

clue.text: Wrinkled — tired out

explanation.surface: Someone looks crumpled and exhausted.
explanation.definitionFit: Creased means crumpled with folds, and in British slang being creased means utterly exhausted.

clue.text: Dash — a fatal thing to do

explanation.surface: An exclamation of annoyance follows a grim warning.
explanation.definitionFit: Hang it is a mild oath like dash it, and hanging is execution by the rope.

clue.text: Modern definition of Christmas

explanation.surface: A dictionary entry for the festive season is called up to date.
explanation.definitionFit: Present-day means contemporary, and Christmas is literally the day of presents.
